warmup.text: The last lesson of fifth grade reading. Choose any poem from this year for Poetry Corner and read it the way it asks to be read. That poem goes in your recording, right after your letter.

words.text: One last look at the year's words: six words you will keep, the word parts that do the work, and a final spelling and grammar check. Then light the last five stops on the year's map.

reading.text: Look back across the whole year. Which book surprised you, which character would you want beside you in sixth grade, and what one sentence about reading do you want to stay true?

assignment.text: Seal and send. Write your envelope, paste your final letter, and record your letter and your poem in Canvas. Then put your booklet together. You finished fifth grade reading.

readnow.text: No new chapter today. Put the year together, then seal and send your letter.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you work. You will use it at the end.
how.why: Seeing one idea across many books is what a whole year of reading gives you.
how.use: You will use it in the Year-End Synthesis.

do: Read the first sentence. It is correct.
Write the second sentence correctly in your reading journal.
Tap See the Answer to check.
how.why: Fixing one sentence at a time trains your eye for your own letter.

do: Read the question.
Write 2 or 3 sentences in your reading journal.
Then go on.
how.why: Thinking first gives you something to say in your letter.

do: Read the poem out loud three times.
Read the tip.
Answer the question in your reading journal.
how.why: Choosing how to read a poem aloud shows what you understand about it.

do: Read the three word groups.
Choose two words from each group.
Define each word and use it in a sentence in the box.
how.why: Words you can use in a sentence are words you own.

do: Write your advice in your reading journal.
Tap the answer for each question.
how.why: Knowing what a word part does is how you read new words.

do: Type the right spelling of each word.
Tap Check My Work.
how.why: These are the words writers miss most.

do: Read the checklist.
Do the journal task.
Tap the right answer for each question.
how.why: One last check, so your letter is ready to send.

do: Read the year in review.
Answer the three questions, one box at a time.
how.why: Looking back is how you see how far you came.

do: Read the three steps.
Write your envelope in the first box.
Paste your final letter in the second box.
how.why: A real letter gets a real envelope.

glossary.meaning: a blob of wax pressed shut with a stamp, used to close a letter

game.title: The Year's Map
game.sub: This week's word game · 5 stops today
game.look: A map of your whole year: five stops, one for each novel's world, from Wethersfield to San Francisco. Each clue asks for a word built from a root you learned while you read that book. A right answer lights the stop.

do: Read the clue.
Tap the word that fits.
A right word lights the stop. Then tap On to the next stop.
how.why: Every root you learned this year still works. Here you use one from each book.

game.doneLine: Twenty stops lit this week. Five books, one year, and every root still works.

rounds.why: im- means not here: not possible.
rounds.miss: Look for the root in the clue's meaning.

rounds.clue: Which word describes a business that has broken down because it ran out of money?
rounds.miss: Look for the root in the clue's meaning.

rounds.clue: Which word names a tool that measures heat?
rounds.why: meter means measure, and therm means heat.
rounds.miss: Look for the root in the clue's meaning.

rounds.clue: Which word means able to feel things strongly?
rounds.miss: Look for the root in the clue's meaning.

rounds.clue: Which word means to lower what something is worth?
rounds.why: val means worth. De- means down.

virtue.name: wisdom
virtue.title: The wisdom you will pass on
virtue.intro: Look back at this year's novels. Tap the piece of wisdom you would pass on to a new 5th grader.

options.t: Isaac: “Be careful what you wish for” (How I Became a Ghost, Chapter 1).
Nat: “when you depend on a book and it has a mistake, you’d have been safer not depending on it” (Carry On, Mr. Bowditch, Chapter 22).
James Otis: “Only that a man can stand up” (Johnny Tremain, Chapter 8).
Jack to Praiseworthy: “We’re partners, sir” (By the Great Horn Spoon!, Chapter 1).

virtue.line: Finish the sentence: I would pass this on because…

art.title: Woman Reading a Letter
art.alt: A painting of a woman in a blue jacket standing by a table in soft window light, holding a letter with both hands and reading it. A large map hangs on the wall behind her.
art.look: Johannes Vermeer painted this woman reading a letter around 1663. She stands very still, holding it with both hands. Someday a new 5th grader will read your letter like this.
